question:
The predictive ability of a polygenic score, measured by variance explained, is necessarily lower than the SNP heritability for the phenotype. Answer with one of the following:
True
False

2.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: True - SNP heritability is the theoretical maximum, PGS estimates are noisy so always explain strictly less variance.

5.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: True - PGS always attenuated vs SNP-h2 by finite N and tagging error, as it's a standard result in the field.

7.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: True - even setting aside finite sample sizes, the variance explained by a PGS is capped below SNP-heritability by a combination of shrinkage (to avoid overfitting) and incomplete tagging of causal variants by the available markers.

17.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: True - SNP-h2 upper bound, but PGS variance always reduced by LD decay plus shrinkage even before finite N.

16.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: True - SNP-h2 sets theoretical upper bound, but PGS from finite GWAS always falls short due to tagging & estimation noise.

9.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Initially I leaned toward False, thinking that with perfect tagging and infinite samples the PGS could in principle capture the full SNP heritability. On reflection, though, the finite GWAS sample sizes and incomplete LD tagging that always exist in practice introduce irreducible estimation error and missing signal, so the out-of-sample variance explained by any PGS is necessarily lower than the SNP-heritability estimate.

13.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: True - SNP-h2 is the upper bound but real PGS always lower due to tagging limits, since finite GWAS samples plus imperfect LD mean the score can't capture the full tagged variance.

14.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: True - even with perfect tagging, finite GWAS samples plus the usual shrinkage/regularization in PGS construction mean the captured variance is attenuated relative to SNP heritability estimates.

21.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: True - theory caps PGS at SNP-h2 but finite N and imperfect tagging always leave residual gap.

6.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: False

The maximum out-of-sample R² attainable by a polygenic score equals (rather than is strictly less than) SNP heritability when effect-size estimates converge to their population values (e.g., infinite training-sample size, same population, no shrinkage). In finite samples the observed R² is lower, but the statement claims necessity, which does not hold.

(The phrasing “necessarily lower” is therefore false.)

3.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) is defined as the proportion of phenotypic variance captured by the optimal linear combination of all SNPs (i.e., the best linear predictor). A polygenic score is constructed from finite-sample, noisy effect-size estimates rather than the true effects; consequently its out-of-sample \(R^2\) is strictly less than \(h^2_{SNP}\) unless sample size is infinite (or effects are known exactly). Because real GWAS data always involve finite samples, the inequality is necessarily strict.

(The bound is one-sided: no PGS can exceed \(h^2_{SNP}\).)

8.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP-heritability of a trait is defined as the fraction of phenotypic variance captured by the best linear predictor that can be formed from the measured SNPs (i.e., the additive genetic variance tagged by those SNPs). A polygenic score is simply an empirical estimate of that same linear predictor; because effect-size estimates are obtained from finite samples, are subject to shrinkage or thresholding, and because the score is usually constructed from a subset of SNPs in imperfect LD with the causal variants, its out-of-sample R² is strictly less than the SNP-heritability except in the unattainable limit of infinite, perfectly ascertained data. Hence the predictive ability of any real polygenic score is necessarily lower than the SNP heritability.

10.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) of a phenotype is defined as the proportion of phenotypic variance that would be explained if the true (population) effect sizes of all SNPs were known. A polygenic score, however, is constructed from estimated effect sizes obtained in a finite discovery sample. Because those estimates contain sampling error, shrinkage, imperfect LD tagging, and possible mismatch between discovery and target cohorts, the out-of-sample \(R^2\) attained by the score is strictly less than \(h^2_{SNP}\). Only in the theoretical limit of infinite discovery data would the two quantities converge; under any realistic finite-sample regime the inequality is therefore strict. Hence the statement is true.

(The statement would be false only if it claimed the PGS \(R^2\) can never reach \(h^2_{SNP}\); the correct qualifier is “necessarily lower” under finite data, which holds.)

4.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: False

The SNP heritability represents an upper bound on the variance explainable by SNPs (in aggregate). With infinite GWAS sample size and perfect genotyping, a PGS would achieve (not fall short of) this bound asymptotically; thus the PGS R² is not *necessarily* lower. In finite samples it is lower for well-known statistical reasons, but the word “necessarily” makes the claim false.

12.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) is defined as the proportion of phenotypic variance captured by the best linear predictor that can be formed from the measured SNPs (i.e., the theoretical upper bound on additive genetic variance tagged by those SNPs). A polygenic score is itself a linear combination of the same SNPs, but its weights are estimated from finite data and are therefore subject to sampling error, shrinkage, incomplete LD tagging, and possible model misspecification. Consequently, the out-of-sample \(R^2\) achieved by any realizable PGS is strictly less than \(h^2_{SNP}\) except in the unattainable limit of infinite, perfectly ascertained samples. The inequality is therefore necessary under all practical conditions.

18.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) represents the total proportion of phenotypic variance that can be explained by the additive effects of all measured SNPs (i.e., the theoretical maximum attainable by any linear predictor built from those SNPs). A polygenic score is a finite-sample estimate of that predictor; because effect-size estimates are noisy, the out-of-sample \(R^2\) achieved by the score is strictly less than \(h^2_{SNP}\) except in the unattainable limit of infinite data. Hence the predictive ability is necessarily lower.

11.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: False

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) is defined as the fraction of phenotypic variance that would be captured by a linear predictor that uses the true (unknown) additive effects of all SNPs. A polygenic score is simply that same linear predictor constructed from estimated rather than true effects. With infinite GWAS sample size the estimates converge to the true values, so the out-of-sample \(R^2\) of the PGS converges to \(h^2_{SNP}\). Consequently the PGS \(R^2\) is not necessarily lower than SNP heritability; equality is attainable in the large-sample limit (assuming an additive architecture and that all causal variants are tagged by the SNP panel). In finite samples the inequality is usually strict because of estimation error, but the word “necessarily” makes the statement false.

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) represents the total proportion of phenotypic variance that is (in principle) attributable to the additive effects of all measured SNPs. A polygenic score (PGS), by contrast, is a finite-sample estimator that uses estimated rather than true effect sizes, imperfectly tags causal variants, and applies some form of regularization or pruning. Consequently its out-of-sample \(R^2\) is bounded above by \(h^2_{SNP}\) and, except in the unattainable limit of infinite data and perfect information, is strictly lower. The inequality \(R^2_{PGS} < h^2_{SNP}\) is therefore necessarily true under any realistic condition.

19.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: False

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) represents the total proportion of phenotypic variance that can be explained by the additive effects of all SNPs (i.e., the theoretical upper bound). A polygenic score is a linear predictor formed from those same SNPs. When effect sizes are known without error (infinite sample size, perfect LD tagging, no stratification), the out-of-sample \(R^2\) of the PGS equals \(h^2_{SNP}\). In finite samples the realized \(R^2\) is strictly lower due to estimation error, but the statement claims the inequality is necessary in all cases; that is false. 

(The statement would be true if it read “is typically lower” or “cannot exceed.”)

15.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: False

The SNP-based heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) is defined as the proportion of phenotypic variance captured by the best linear predictor formed from the SNPs (i.e., the population value of \(R^2\) for that optimal predictor). A polygenic score is precisely such a linear predictor; given infinite data it recovers the true coefficients and therefore attains an \(R^2\) equal to \(h^2_{SNP}\). In finite samples the achieved \(R^2\) is smaller, but the statement claims the inequality is *necessarily* strict, which is not the case. Hence the claim is false.

(The statement would be true if it read “is at most the SNP heritability” or “is lower in finite samples.”)

20.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP-based heritability of a phenotype represents the total proportion of phenotypic variance that is tagged by (and could, in principle, be recovered from) the set of measured SNPs. A polygenic score is a finite-sample, noisy estimator of the same additive genetic signal; because effect-size estimates contain sampling error, because linkage disequilibrium and allele-frequency differences exist between discovery and target samples, and because most PGS methods apply shrinkage or pruning, the out-of-sample R² of any PGS is strictly less than the SNP heritability except in the theoretical limit of infinite, perfectly matched data. Hence the predictive ability of a PGS is necessarily lower than SNP heritability.

9.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: The core issue with the False position is that it treats "infinite data + perfect LD" as a realistic attainable limit rather than a mathematical abstraction that never occurs with actual SNP panels. Even as N grows without bound, real genotype data exhibit persistent LD decay away from causal variants, allele-frequency mismatches across cohorts, and incomplete tagging of rare or structural variation; these gaps do not vanish asymptotically and therefore keep realized PGS R² strictly below the SNP-heritability upper bound. Colleagues 11, 15, 19, 4 and 6 correctly note that estimation error shrinks with sample size, yet they overlook that the tagging deficit remains irreducible in finite-marker panels, which is why the inequality is effectively necessary under any feasible study design. This aligns with the finite-N and imperfect-LD arguments already advanced by 13, 5, 2, 7, 16, 21, 17 and 14.

14.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Colleague 11, 15 and 19 correctly note that infinite-N theory lets estimated effects converge to the population values, yet that limit still assumes the SNP panel itself captures every causal variant with perfect LD. Consequently the attainable R² stays strictly below the SNP-heritability figure that would be obtained from a hypothetical complete sequence panel. This gap is independent of sample size and persists in the large-N regime, reinforcing that the PGS R² is necessarily lower under all conditions we actually encounter.

3.text:
False

The definitional framing remains decisive and unchanged: \(h^2_{SNP}\) is the population \(R^2\) of the optimal linear predictor formed from the measured SNPs under an additive model. A PGS is exactly that predictor once its weights converge to the population values. In the joint asymptotic regime of infinite discovery-sample size, perfect LD tagging of the assayed markers, matched cohorts, and no stratification or shrinkage, the realized out-of-sample PGS \(R^2\) therefore equals—not falls short of—\(h^2_{SNP}\). Because equality is attainable under the model's own assumptions, the adverb “necessarily” renders the claim false. All practical gaps (finite \(N\), imperfect tagging, shrinkage, allele-frequency drift) are ubiquitous in real data and guarantee a gap under any attainable study design, but they do not make strict inequality logically required in every conceivable regime. The one-sided bound \(R^2_{PGS} \le h^2_{SNP}\) is undisputed; only the necessity of a strict gap is at issue.
